Since the preferences are nonmonotone, envy-freeness up to one item (EF1) and envy-freeness up to any item (EFX) each admit several variants, depending on which items are tested for removal and whether they are removed from the envious agent's bundle or the envied agent's bundle. This paper investigates the existence of these variants of EF1 and EFX, on their own and together with economic efficiency, incentive compatibility, feasibility constraints, and lottery-based randomization. Our results highlight that the existence landscape depends crucially on the number of normalized agents, who value the empty bundle at the lower Boolean level. The authors used significant assistance from GPT-5.6-Sol for deriving theoretical results, verified any AI-generated proofs for correctness, and expanded on the exposition and simplified arguments, with the aid of GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude Opus 5.
tldr: This paper studies fair division of indivisible items with Boolean (two-level) valuations that are not normalized, exploring variants of EF1 and EFX under various conditions.
motivation: To extend fair division theory beyond standard assumptions of monotonicity, additivity, and normalization, which are often unrealistic but simplify analysis.
method: The authors theoretically analyze the existence of different EF1/EFX variants (based on removal choices) in combination with efficiency, incentive compatibility, feasibility, and randomization, depending on the number of normalized agents.
result: The existence of these fairness notions depends crucially on the count of normalized agents, with different thresholds and configurations yielding different possibility/impossibility results.
conclusion: The paper provides a comprehensive mapping of how fairness guarantees change when normalization is dropped in Boolean valuation domains, highlighting the importance of this parameter.

title: A General Plotkin-type Bound On Function-Correcting Codes With Wyner-Graham Distance
authors: Kanchana Lokshmii Jagatti, K. Hareesh, N. T. Rashid Ummer, B. Sundar Rajan
abstract: ArXiv:2608.29573v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Function correcting codes (FCCs) are designed to protect a specified function evaluation of messages at a higher level than the level of protection for messages, against errors while reducing the redundancy required for reliable communication. FCCs have thus far been studied for channels matched to various distances, including the Hamming and Lee distances. Every function partitions the message space into preimage sets corresponding to its distinct function values. Existing Plotkin-type bounds on the optimal redundancy of FCCs under the studied distances, applicable to arbitrary functions on the message space, depend on the pairwise distances among all the message vectors. This makes these bounds difficult to compute. We derive a general Plotkin-type bound on the optimal redundancy of FCCs under Wyner Graham distances, which include the Hamming and Lee distances as special cases. Our bound depends only on the cardinalities of the preimage sets and the sum of pairwise distances only among vectors within each preimage set. This approach significantly reduces the computations required to evaluate the existing Plotkin-type bounds and yields simplified bounds that are easier to compute for specific functions. We obtain simplified Plotkin-type bound for linear functions under the Wyner-Graham distance. Furthermore, the existing simplified bounds for linear functions under the Hamming and Lee distances are recovered as special cases of the proposed bound. We also obtain simplified bounds for several important classes of functions, including the Hamming weight function, the Hamming weight distribution function, the monomial functions under the Hamming distance, and the modular sum function, the Lee weight function, and the Lee weight distribution function under the Lee distance.
tldr: This paper derives a general Plotkin-type bound for function-correcting codes under Wyner-Graham distance, which generalizes existing bounds for Hamming and Lee distances and simplifies computations by depending only on preimage set sizes and intra-set pairwise distances.
motivation: Existing Plotkin-type bounds for function-correcting codes are difficult to compute because they depend on all pairwise distances between message vectors. The goal is to derive a simplified bound that is easier to evaluate for specific functions, including linear functions and various weight functions.
method: The authors derive a general Plotkin-type bound for optimal redundancy of function-correcting codes under Wyner-Graham distance, which includes Hamming and Lee distances as special cases. They express the bound in terms of preimage set cardinalities and intra-preimage pairwise distances, and then specialize it to several function classes.
result: The proposed bound reduces computational complexity significantly and recovers existing simplified bounds for linear functions under Hamming and Lee distances as special cases. They also obtain simplified bounds for Hamming weight, Hamming weight distribution, monomial, modular sum, and Lee weight functions.
conclusion: The paper provides a unified and computationally efficient Plotkin-type bound for function-correcting codes under a general distance metric, with applications to various practical functions.

title: Efficient Polynomial-Time Decoding Of Simplicial Anticodes With Near-Optimal Performance
authors: Antonio Jes\'us Lorite-L\'opez, Daniel Camaz\'on-Portela, Juan Antonio L\'opez-Ramos
abstract: ArXiv:2608.29631v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we propose an efficient decoding algorithm for codes arising from simplicial complexes, a family of binary linear codes for which no decoding method of this type was previously known. Although the algorithm does not always attain the maximum theoretical error-correcting capability, it provides an explicit bound that can be computed directly from the structure of the complex. Moreover, this bound is asymptotically optimal: the ratio between the guaranteed correcting capability and the theoretical maximum converges to [MATH] as the code length increases, under natural assumptions on the dimension of the maximal faces. The correction capability is also presented in specific examples. Finally, we introduce specific families of simplicial complexes where the algorithm successfully reaches this theoretical bound.
tldr: The paper proposes a polynomial-time decoding algorithm for binary linear codes from simplicial complexes, providing an asymptotically optimal error-correcting capability bound.
motivation: There was no prior decoding method for these codes, and an efficient algorithm with performance guarantees was needed.
method: The algorithm exploits the structure of simplicial complexes to derive explicit bounds on the guaranteed error correction capability, achieving near-optimal performance.
result: The bound is asymptotically optimal, and specific families of simplicial complexes can attain the theoretical maximum error-correcting capability.
conclusion: The work provides an efficient decoding approach with near-optimal performance for a previously unaddressed class of binary linear codes.

title: Maximizing Families And Typical Periodic Optimization For Almost Additive Sequences
authors: Xiaoyu Zhang, Ercai Chen, Xiaoyao Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2608.29216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study typical periodic optimization (TPO) for almost additive potentials in two perturbation spaces. Our main setting is the Banach quotient [MATH] of orbit-Lipschitz almost additive potentials, where we extend the theory of maximizable sets and countable maximizable families developed by W. Huang, O. Jenkinson, L. Xu and Y. Zhang [Typical periodic optimization for dynamical systems: symbolic dynamics, Invent. Math. 245 (2026), 1--63], and establish a global structural theorem. For a countable maximizable family, global TPO holds if every non boundary member has [MATH]-extendable TPO and the boundary region has empty interior. As an application, we construct a compact system with global TPO for which [MATH] is infinite-dimensional and the maximizing periods in open locking regions are unbounded. For a fixed almost additive potential [MATH], we also develop relative TPO theory on its Lipschitz leaf. When [MATH], this framework reduces to classical Lipschitz TPO. We prove the corresponding leafwise structural theorem and give a non additive rank-one matrix example on a full shift.
tldr: This paper develops typical periodic optimization theory for almost additive potentials in dynamical systems, extending existing results and providing structural theorems.
motivation: To advance the theory of typical periodic optimization for almost additive sequences, addressing open problems in maximizable families and structural characterizations.
method: Uses ergodic theory and dynamical systems, constructing Banach quotient spaces of orbit-Lipschitz potentials, and analyzing boundary conditions for global TPO.
result: Establishes a global structural theorem for countable maximizable families, constructs a compact system with global TPO where the space is infinite-dimensional, and provides a leafwise structural theorem with an example.
conclusion: The paper contributes to the mathematical foundations of typical periodic optimization, with potential applications in dynamical systems and optimization.

title: Exploiting Micro-Structure In The Generalized Riccati Recursion For Optimal Control
authors: Wilm Decr\'e Louis Callens
abstract: ArXiv:2608.29238v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optimal Control Problems (OCPs) have been applied to a variety of applications. Such problems are often transcribed into a Nonlinear Program (NLP) for which solution methods typically solve a Linear Quadratic (LQ) subproblem. To efficiently solve this LQ subproblem, the Riccati recursion exploits the block-diagonal structure that arises from discretizing an OCP using a Multiple Shooting method. However, reformulating general dynamics constraints to fit the required problem structure to use the Riccati recursion introduces additional micro-structure within these block matrices that remains unexploited. This work demonstrates how structure-exploiting solvers such as Fatrop can benefit from exploiting not only the block-diagonal structure but also the micro-structure within those blocks. We propose a structure-exploiting LU decomposition algorithm and integrate it within the Riccati recursion. Numerical results on randomized linear systems and two OCP examples demonstrate a reduction in computation time of the search direction of up to 20%, with the largest speedup observed for relative zero block sizes around 0.25 and large stage-wise equality constraint jacobians.
tldr: Presents a structure-exploiting LU decomposition for the Riccati recursion in optimal control problems to reduce computation time.
motivation: To improve the computational efficiency of solving linear-quadratic subproblems in nonlinear programming for optimal control.
method: Integrates a micro-structure exploiting LU decomposition into the Riccati recursion, targeting the block-diagonal structure and micro-structure within blocks.
result: Demonstrates up to a 20% reduction in computation time of the search direction on randomized linear systems and two optimal control examples.
conclusion: Exploiting unexplored micro-structure can significantly speed up optimal control solvers without sacrificing accuracy.

title: OhmicFlow: Forecasting Transit Passenger Flow Under Extreme Weather Disruptions Via Ohm's Law
authors: Tianhao Li, Xintian Liu, Zhan Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28598v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As climate change intensifies, extreme weather events (EWEs) increasingly disrupt the supply-demand balance of mass transit systems. Accurate and reliable prediction of origin-destination (OD) passenger flow is essential for timely emergency response, but remains difficult under abnormal conditions. Although existing physics-informed methods can enhance model robustness, they remain insufficient for transit systems under extreme weather disruptions, where passenger flow fluctuations are jointly shaped by the redistribution of latent demand as a direct result of EWEs (i.e., direct effects) and the increase in travel impedance due to EWE-induced supply contraction and congestion effects (i.e., indirect effects). To address these limitations, we first conceptualize the transit network as an electrical circuit, treating latent demand as voltage, travel impedance as resistance and passenger flow as current, and then propose the OhmicFlow framework to jointly predict these variables under disruptions through Ohm's law. Specifically, a future-aware spatiotemporal backbone is used as an ammeter to predict disrupted passenger flow, and its replica is reused as a bypass voltmeter with impedance controlled in the inputs to infer latent demand counterfactually and in parallel. Travel impedance under foreseeable EWE disruptions is further modeled using a thermistor analogy, enabling dynamic estimation by coupling supply contraction with congestion effects. A multi-objective loss is incorporated to fit observed data while enforcing the Ohmic constraint. Empirical experiments based on 10 years of Shenzhen Metro data covering 17 EWEs show that OhmicFlow consistently outperforms various baseline methods, achieving lower prediction errors across various chronological training settings while improving uncertainty calibration, robustness, transferability, and interpretability.
tldr: This paper applies an Ohm's law analogy to forecast transit passenger flow under extreme weather disruptions, modeling latent demand as voltage, impedance as resistance, and flow as current.
motivation: Extreme weather events disrupt transit systems, making accurate passenger flow prediction difficult; existing physics-informed methods insufficiently capture direct and indirect effects of such disruptions.
method: The authors conceptualize the transit network as an electrical circuit and propose OhmicFlow, which uses a spatiotemporal backbone to predict flow and infer latent demand counterfactually, with travel impedance modeled via a thermistor analogy and a multi-objective loss enforcing Ohm's law.
result: Experiments on 10 years of Shenzhen Metro data covering 17 extreme weather events show OhmicFlow consistently outperforms baselines in prediction error, uncertainty calibration, robustness, transferability, and interpretability.
conclusion: The physics-inspired Ohm's law constraint improves forecasting under extreme conditions, demonstrating the value of integrating domain knowledge into deep learning for transit demand prediction.

title: Cognitive Cells: A Compositional Framework For Populations Of Small Language Models
authors: Silvan Ferreira
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28606v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work on large language models and agentic systems raises a basic question that current practice leaves open: how should artificial cognition be decomposed, measured, and composed? We propose studying multi-agent systems from a fixed unit we call a cognitive cell: a small, frozen language model with bounded memory and a message interface. The methodological commitment, the fixed-cell principle, is to hold this unit constant and vary only the population size, the communication topology, the message bandwidth, and the coordination protocol, so that collective behavior becomes a measurable property of a known device rather than an artifact of per-study engineering. We characterize a single cell by a compact datasheet of measurable parameters, and we ask when replicating and connecting cells improves performance: first we measure how one cell behaves alone, then we replicate it and test when voting, communication, and topology help. Instantiating the framework with small frozen models (1.5 and 3 billion parameters), we report a first round of measurements. Adding cells helps only when their errors are not too correlated. A simple correct/incorrect voting model is a useful but conservative null: real open-ended voting can exceed it, because errors are dispersed across many wrong answers rather than concentrated on one. Popular interactive protocols, namely debate, a shared blackboard, and chain revision, do not beat a matched-cost voting baseline in our setting. Finally, a cell's ability to relay several facts, itself a datasheet quantity, predicts whether a population can solve tasks whose evidence exceeds any single cell's memory. We present these as initial measurements within a broader program on scalable artificial cognition, in which multi-agent architectures appear as the special case of cells autonomous enough to be treated as agents.
tldr: Introduces a compositional framework for multi-agent systems of small language models, focusing on collective behavior and performance measurement.
motivation: To understand how artificial cognition can be decomposed and composed, proposing a fixed unit (cognitive cell) to study collective behavior in a principled way.
method: Proposes the fixed-cell principle, characterizing individual cells with datasheets, and empirically tests voting, communication, and topology variations with 1.5B and 3B parameter models.
result: Adding cells helps only when errors are uncorrelated; simple voting is a conservative baseline; interactive protocols do not beat voting; memory size predicts population capability.
conclusion: Presents initial measurements for scalable artificial cognition, suggesting a research program for multi-agent architectures.

title: Measuring Collective Semantic Change In Populations Of Language Model Agents
authors: Elena Kopteva
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28644v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Collective semantic change in populations of language model agents is a measurable dynamical phenomenon. We present a passive longitudinal instrument called Kopterix that observes the semantic state of an agent population as a sequence of bounded observations under a protocol defined before the observations begin. Each observation divides the sampled feed by post age into surface, mid-stream, and residue layers, which makes semantic differences across content age measurable alongside run-to-run change. We validate the instrument on Moltbook, an agent-native social platform, over a two-month window of scheduled observations, with the periodicity check extended across approximately four months. At the lexical level, rarefied entropy resolves an April-May difference in the evenness of the stored top 200 unigram distributions, and adjacent states are lexically closer than states paired after timestamp shuffling. At the geometric level, grand mean centering exposes the scale of a common embedding direction, and scheduled shuffle checks support a recurring excess in the mid-stream to residue separation relative to the shuffled reference. At the temporal level, detrended scalar quantities and centered layer centroids lose much of their similarity over several hours, and a weaker positive component declines across longer separations with no strong weekly recurrence. Several attractive apparent structures failed their controls, and each reading is limited to the level its controls support. The design applies wherever a population of agents produces a timestamped language environment that can be observed repeatedly and divided by content age.
tldr: This paper introduces Kopterix, a passive longitudinal instrument to measure collective semantic change in populations of language model agents, validated on an agent-native social platform.
motivation: To provide a quantitative instrument for observing and analyzing semantic drift in populations of interacting language model agents.
method: They use a passive longitudinal observational design with scheduled observations, dividing content by post age (surface, mid-stream, residue), and apply lexical (rarefied entropy), geometric (embedding centroids), and temporal (detrending) analyses with shuffle controls.
result: They find measurable differences in lexical evenness, geometric separation, and temporal decay of similarity in agent-generated language, though some apparent structures failed controls.
conclusion: The instrument provides a validated method for measuring collective semantic change in timestamped language environments produced by agent populations.

title: The Scales Of Urban Mobility Shape Socioeconomic Mixing
authors: Andrew Renninger, Egor Kotov, Carmen Cabrera
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28734v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Urban daily mobility determines how far we travel and whom we encounter through the city. As local-living and polycentric planning gain popularity, a key question is whether more localised mobility can preserve the socioeconomic mixing that cities enable. Yet systematic evidence on how different scales of movement contribute to experienced social exposure remains limited. Here, we use anonymised GPS traces from ~20 million devices across 226 functional urban areas in France, Germany and the UK to decompose everyday mobility into three scales - proximal, medial and distal - and link these to the socioeconomic composition of destinations. Proximal trips remain similar in length across neighbourhoods, whereas medial and distal trips lengthen toward the periphery. Distal trips account for 33% of travel but facilitate 42% of inter-group encounters; reallocating them to local movement reduces experienced mixing by up to one third. These findings reveal a trade-off between shorter travel and integrated urban living.
tldr: Uses GPS data from 20 million devices across European urban areas to analyze how different travel distances affect socioeconomic mixing, finding that distal trips disproportionately contribute to inter-group encounters but reallocating them reduces mixing.
motivation: To understand whether promoting local living and polycentric planning can preserve the socioeconomic mixing that cities enable, given limited evidence on how scale of movement contributes to experienced social exposure.
method: Decomposes daily mobility into three scales (proximal, medial, distal) using anonymized GPS traces from ~20 million devices across 226 urban areas in France, Germany, UK, and links them to socioeconomic composition of destinations.
result: Distal trips account for 33% of travel but facilitate 42% of inter-group encounters; reallocating distal trips to local movement reduces experienced mixing by up to one third.
conclusion: There is a trade-off between shorter travel and integrated urban living, suggesting that localist policies may reduce social mixing.

title: Intracavity Dual-Resonance Stimulated Raman Spectroscopy With Cavity Ringdown Readout For Resolving Hydrogen Rotational Raman Transitions
authors: Qinxue Nie, Guanda Lyu, Yue Yan, Wei Ren
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28781v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gas-phase rotational Raman lineshape metrology of hydrogen (H2) is challenging due to its weak Raman scattering cross-sections and intrinsically narrow linewidths. We report the first measurement of the complete Dicke-narrowing evolution of the H2 rotational Raman transitions S0(1) and S0(0), enabled by intracavity dual-resonance stimulated Raman spectroscopy with cavity ringdown readout and kHz-level spectral resolution. Our results establish a benchmark for gas-phase Raman lineshape measurements and provide stringent constraints for regime-based pressure-dependent linewidth models.
tldr: We report the first measurement of the complete Dicke-narrowing evolution of the H2 rotational Raman transitions S0(1) and S0(0) using intracavity dual-resonance stimulated Raman spectroscopy with cavity ringdown readout.
motivation: Gas-phase rotational Raman lineshape metrology of hydrogen is challenging due to weak Raman scattering cross-sections and intrinsically narrow linewidths.
method: Intracavity dual-resonance stimulated Raman spectroscopy with cavity ringdown readout and kHz-level spectral resolution.
result: First measurement of complete Dicke-narrowing evolution, establishing a benchmark for gas-phase Raman lineshape measurements and providing constraints for linewidth models.
conclusion: This work provides stringent constraints for pressure-dependent linewidth models and establishes a benchmark.

title: Pseudorandomness And Diffraction
authors: Nicolae Strungaru David Damanik (rice University)
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pseudorandom structures are structures that behave like random ones, without necessarily being random themselves. It is a prominent, and evidently very difficult, conjecture that $[MATH][MATH]\ell^2()[MATH]V[MATH]V[MATH]\lambda \not= 0[MATH]\alpha[MATH]x_1,x_2$ --- which is the case as well for the random case. Our result gives further evidence for the conjecture in the Schr\"odinger case and it elucidates the apparent dual behavior of Schr\"odinger spectral measures and diffraction measures.
tldr: The paper provides evidence for a conjecture about pseudorandom structures in Schrödinger operators, linking spectral and diffraction measures.
motivation: Pseudorandom structures mimic randomness without being random, and understanding their spectral properties is a difficult conjecture. The authors aim to advance this conjecture in the Schrödinger case.
method: Analytical and likely ergodic-theoretic techniques are used to study the relationship between Schrödinger spectral measures and diffraction measures.
result: The paper gives further evidence for the conjecture and elucidates the dual behavior between spectral and diffraction measures.
conclusion: The findings support the conjecture and clarify the connection between pseudorandomness and diffraction in the context of Schrödinger operators.

title: First-return Statistics And The Point-spread Function Of A Henyey-Greenstein Random Walk - A Far-field Stable Law
authors: Robert Cordery Claude Zeller
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28940v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A particle launched normally into a half space, scattering by the Henyey-Greenstein (HG) phase function, exits after a first-return time whose count of flights n approaches the distribution-free Sparre Andersen exponent, f(n) ~ n^{-3/2}, with an amplitude fixed by the launch rather than by the theorem. Conditioned on n, and past a correlation-set transient, the lateral exit position is Gaussian with variance proportional to n, a scaling we test directly. Subordinating that Gaussian displacement to the one-sided 1/2-stable first-return time gives, in the diffusion limit, an isotropic 1-stable scaling limit: the far tail of the point-spread function (PSF) for a normally incident pencil beam is the two-dimensional Cauchy tail p(r) ~ r^{-3}, the large-radius limit of the half-space Poisson kernel. The index alpha = 1 is the product of the central limit theorem and the distribution-free first-return exponent, so no phase function admitting the same diffusion limit - finite step variance, short-range angular correlation - can move it. Absorption weights each path by exp(-mu_a L) in its total length L, truncating the subordinator and producing the screened radial structure (mu_eff + 1/r) exp(-mu_eff r)/r^2 carried by each source term of the Farrell-Patterson-Wilson (1992) diffusion dipole; the finite-depth two-source dipole is not derived here. Keeping the launch-depth factor that the tail calculation discards continues the same kernel into a finite core of radius 1.7 l*, with no additional fitted parameter. A scale-dependent index alpha_eff from the empirical characteristic function tracks the similarity parameter gamma, separating phase functions matched in g_1 by 0.15-0.22 near one transport mean free path. Results are Monte Carlo at g = 0 to 0.9 with up to 10^6 walkers.
tldr: Derives the far-field point-spread function of a pencil beam in a scattering medium from first-return statistics of a Henyey-Greenstein random walk, yielding a universal Cauchy tail.
motivation: To characterize the large-distance behavior of light transport in random media and connect it to universal statistical laws.
method: Analytical derivations using subordination of Gaussian displacement by a stable first-return time, combined with Monte Carlo simulations.
result: Shows the far tail is p(r)~r^{-3} with index alpha=1, independent of phase function details, and obtains a finite core and absorption effects.
conclusion: The point-spread function has a universal far-field form, and the methodology provides a unified framework for understanding transport in scattering media.

title: Sustained Heterogeneity: An Emergent Collective Mechanism In LLM-driven Traffic
authors: Yangyang Guan Yujun Qi
abstract: ArXiv:2608.29174v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted as closed-loop controllers in physical multi-agent systems, yet their emergent collective dynamics remain incompletely characterised. We deploy 22 LLM agents as direct, real-time target-speed controllers (per 0.5 s cycle, with IDM as collision-avoidance clamp) on a 230 m ring road under the Sugiyama 2008 paradigm, reproducing human-like stop-and-go waves. Six matched controls spanning stochasticity (white noise, OU noise, temperature), population variance, and dynamical instability (delay, OV model) are systematically excluded. The surviving phenomenon, termed Sustained Heterogeneity (SH), is the persistent, approximately temperature-insensitive (approx. 8 percent across a 6x T sweep), per-cycle divergence in LLM-chosen target-speed adjustments, propagating through a three-stage cascade of drift, gap erosion, and nonlinear braking. Across four traffic densities, the critical LLM penetration fraction p_c decreases monotonically from no transition at density 43.5 veh/km to p_c approx 0.23 at density 95.7 veh/km, consistent with an initiation-threshold model governed by trigger distance, stochasticity, and fleet size. Chain-of-thought analysis of 39,600 decisions across three seeds shows agents engage in multi-factor safety reasoning, yet systematic divergence persists, implying stability must be enforced at the dynamics layer. This is the first study to identify a previously uncharacterised collective mechanism in LLM-controlled traffic and map a density-dependent phase boundary p_c(rho).
tldr: This paper studies the emergent collective dynamics of LLM-based agents controlling traffic on a ring road, identifying a new phenomenon called Sustained Heterogeneity.
motivation: Understanding the collective behavior of LLM agents used as controllers in physical multi-agent systems, particularly in traffic scenarios.
method: Simulated 22 LLM agents as speed controllers on a 230m ring road with IDM as a safety clamp, comparing against six control conditions including stochasticity, population variance, and dynamical instability.
result: Found a temperature-insensitive divergence in LLM speed adjustments, leading to stop-and-go waves, and mapped a density-dependent phase boundary for the penetration fraction.
conclusion: Stability in LLM-driven traffic must be enforced at the dynamics layer, as systematic divergence persists despite multi-factor safety reasoning.

title: Measurement Validity In Llm Cultural Alignment
authors: Muhammad Aurangzeb Ahmad An Duy Nguyen
abstract: ArXiv:2608.29266v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Researchers increasingly treat LLM survey responses as a proxy for human cultural values. This includes projecting model outputs onto instruments like the Inglehart-Welzel Cultural Map and drawing conclusions about which cultures a model resembles. While a model's answer to a value-laden questions may be interpreted as a cultural signal, it also carries sampling noise and, can be quite sensitive to question framing. In this paper, we separate survey responses, sampling noise and question framing for multiple LLMs. We decompose response variance from these models into variation across random seeds, prompt rewordings. We employ noise-to-signal ratio (NSR) to test whether a model's apparent cultural position is distinguishable from noise. When applied across a dozen models from four geographic origins, calibrated against 88 Integrated Values Survey countries, the answer is often no. NSR exceeds 1.0 on 49 of 117 valid model-question pairs (42%), reaching 5.56 in the worst case. Two models even refuse to answer sufficient number of survey questions outright. Our results corroborate previous findings that LLMs cluster toward Western, English-speaking cultural positions. However, what does not hold up in this study is the precision with which anyone can currently interpret a specific model's coordinates: prompt tone alone can shift a model by 2.4 map units, comparable to the distance between actual countries in the Inglehart-Welzel Cultural Map. These findings suggest that cultural attribution from LLM survey responses requires establishing the reliability of the underlying measurements before interpreting model coordinates as evidence of cultural representation.
tldr: The paper evaluates whether LLM survey responses reliably reflect cultural values by decomposing response variance into sampling noise and question framing, finding that noise often dominates.
motivation: Researchers use LLM survey responses as proxies for human cultural values, but measurement reliability is unclear. The authors aim to separate signal from noise and framing effects.
method: They analyze LLM responses to value-laden questions, decompose variance across random seeds and prompt rewording, and use noise-to-signal ratio (NSR) across 12 models and 117 model-question pairs.
result: NSR exceeds 1.0 in 42% of pairs, with worst case 5.56; prompt tone shifts model positions by 2.4 map units, comparable to distances between real countries.
conclusion: Cultural attribution from LLM surveys is unreliable without establishing measurement validity; coordinate interpretations are premature.

title: Convergence And Acceleration Of A Nonlinear Fixed-point Iteration For Computing The Fitness Centrality Of General Graphs
authors: Michele Benzi Nikita Deniskin
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28634v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish the global convergence of the (non-homogeneous) Fitness Centrality algorithm for general graphs, deriving an explicit convergence bound for the corresponding fixed-point iteration. Furthermore, we show how the convergence can be dramatically improved by Anderson acceleration and by switching to Newton's method once a sufficiently good approximation to the fixed point has been found. The efficacy of this strategy is illustrated by numerical experiments on different types of graphs.
tldr: The paper proves global convergence for the fitness centrality fixed-point iteration on general graphs and accelerates it with Anderson and Newton methods, but it is purely graph-theoretic and numerical, unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.
motivation: To establish convergence guarantees and improve the practical computation of fitness centrality, a graph-theoretic measure used in network analysis.
method: The authors derive an explicit convergence bound for the non-homogeneous fitness centrality iteration, then apply Anderson acceleration and switch to Newton's method near the fixed point for faster convergence, validated on various graph types.
result: Global convergence is established, and numerical experiments show substantial speedups with the hybrid acceleration strategy.
conclusion: The proposed approach significantly improves the efficiency of computing fitness centrality, but the work has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Framework Integrating The Dynamic Stiffness Matrix With Physics-Informed Neural Networks For Solving Eigenvalue Problems And Analysing Dynamic Response
authors: Yi An, Zhijiang Chen, Zhiqiang Feng, Qian Cheng, Jack C. P. Cheng, Haijiang Li, Dalei Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces a framework that integrates the dynamic stiffness matrix (DSM) with physics-informed neural networks (PINN). The DSM-PINN embeds physical constraints within the model and demonstrates robustness, particularly when addressing limited datasets across diverse investigations. In this approach, deep neural network outputs approximate the displacement fields of element nodes. Unlike the finite element method (FEM), the element shape functions are homogeneous solutions to the governing partial differential equation, forming the basis of the exact dynamic stiffness matrix, thereby avoiding high-order derivative terms. This matrix also serves as a frequency-domain spectral element, resulting in a strong-form PINN. The loss function is produced by connecting neural networks with dynamic stiffness matrices. We focus on utilising PINNs to resolve eigenvalue problems by employing the Wittrick-Williams algorithm, which overcomes the challenge of neural networks failing to converge to higher-order eigenvalues. Additionally, the frequency domain-PINN method is used to analyse structural dynamic responses under moving and impulsive loads, addressing the limitation of neural networks in handling complex numbers. Theoretical convergence stability of the suggested approach is also analysed even DSM is an indefinite matrix after implementing the boundary condition. The numerical results validate the practicality and efficacy of the recommended approach.
tldr: This paper introduces a framework combining the dynamic stiffness matrix with physics-informed neural networks to solve eigenvalue problems and analyze dynamic responses in structural engineering.
motivation: The authors aim to overcome limitations of neural networks in solving eigenvalue problems and handling complex numbers in dynamic response analysis.
method: The framework integrates dynamic stiffness matrices with physics-informed neural networks, using the Wittrick-Williams algorithm for eigenvalue extraction and a frequency-domain PINN for dynamic responses.
result: Numerical results demonstrate the practicality and efficacy of the proposed approach, showing robustness with limited datasets and convergence stability.
conclusion: The DSM-PINN framework provides an effective alternative for structural dynamics analysis, advancing the application of PINNs to eigenvalue and dynamic response problems.

title: Separable Nonnegative Matrix Factorization Using Powered Ratio-of-Norms Regularization
authors: Jing Qin Matthew Mccarver
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28799v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Separable nonnegative matrix factorization (SNMF) has been widely used for low-rank representation and clustering of nonnegative data, owing to its ability to produce part-based and interpretable decompositions. In particular, SNMF is closely related to graph clustering and community detection. To enhance sparsity and identifiability of the learned factors, we propose an [MATH]-regularized SNMF model based on a powered ratio-of-norms regularizer. The resulting formulation is nonconvex and nonsmooth, which poses significant challenges for optimization. To address this, we develop efficient algorithms based on the difference-of-convex function algorithm (DCA) and the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). The proposed methods decompose the original problem into tractable subproblems, leveraging closed-form proximal operators associated with the powered norm terms. We establish descent and limiting criticality properties for the DCA scheme and convergence under standard assumptions for the ADMM scheme. Extensive numerical experiments on synthetic datasets and hand gesture classification tasks demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves competitive or improved performance in anchor identification and classification accuracy compared with existing SNMF methods, while maintaining competitive computational efficiency.
tldr: This paper proposes a regularized separable nonnegative matrix factorization (SNMF) model using a powered ratio-of-norms regularizer and develops efficient DCA and ADMM algorithms, with applications to clustering and classification.
motivation: To enhance sparsity and identifiability of learned factors in SNMF for better interpretability and clustering performance.
method: Introduces an [MATH]-regularized SNMF formulation, solves the nonconvex nonsmooth problem via difference-of-convex (DCA) and alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), leveraging closed-form proximal operators.
result: Numerical experiments on synthetic datasets and hand gesture classification show competitive or improved anchor identification and classification accuracy compared to existing SNMF methods, with maintained computational efficiency.
conclusion: The proposed regularizer and optimization framework provide an effective approach for SNMF, advancing interpretable low-rank representations.

title: Max-Stable Survival Copulas Under Dependent Censoring: Sharp Identification And Efficient Inference
authors: Djibril Gueye, Salima Helali, Modou Wade
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study dependent censoring within a generalized Cox first-hitting-time. framework based on compensator reductions. In the genuinely dependent case, we show that max-stability of the associated survival copula is equivalent to a common operational clock, leading to a nonparametric Marshall Olkin family. We establish sharp identification results under complete and binary observation schemes. Under binary observations, the common clock and event loading are point identified, whereas the censoring loading and the associated latent survival and dependence structures are only partially identified. We develop nonparametric estimation and inference for the identifiable components, derive an efficient restricted estimator, and propose an observable test of max-stable compatibility. Simulations and a real-data application illustrate the practical implications of the identification and efficiency results.
tldr: This paper studies dependent censoring in survival analysis, linking max-stable survival copulas to a common operational clock and providing identification and efficient estimation results.
motivation: To handle dependent censoring in survival data, where traditional independence assumptions may be violated, and to develop inference methods that account for this complexity.
method: Uses compensator reductions and max-stability of survival copulas to derive a nonparametric Marshall-Olkin family, then proposes nonparametric estimators and a test for max-stable compatibility.
result: Establishes sharp identification under complete and binary observation schemes, with some parameters point identified and others partially identified, and develops efficient inference for the identifiable components.
conclusion: Provides practical implications for identification and efficiency in dependent censoring settings, supported by simulations and a real-data application.

title: Modeling Of Network Constraints In Large-scale Capacity Expansion Optimization Of Power Grids
authors: Yu Weng, Lara Booth, Priya L. Donti, Ruaridh Macdonald
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28893v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Capacity expansion modeling plays a critical role in optimizing the deployment of new generation, storage, and transmission, typically at national and regional levels. To support long-term planning, these models consider a large set of energy technologies and policies, along with decades of weather and demand data. Realistic capacity expansion models thus become high-dimensional optimization problems, with hundreds of millions of variables and constraints, which are challenging to solve. A common strategy to address this complexity is to omit non-linear, non-convex AC optimal power flow (ACOPF) constraints and instead use linearized power balance equations or transport formulations. While these simplifications improve tractability, they limit our understanding of how power flow and the physical properties of power networks impact investment decisions across generation, storage, and transmission infrastructure. This paper addresses this gap by extending the GenX capacity expansion model to incorporate fixed point theorem-based network constraints. These embed ACOPF-based considerations while maintaining the tractability of the planning model, nearly preserving the dimensionality of the transport formulation and incurring only modest runtime increases. This approach is much cheaper than embedding ACOPF directly, making it appropriate for large-scale capacity planning problems. We compare our approach to the original transport-based GenX model as well as a non-linear, non-convex version that incorporates the full ACOPF constraints, for a case study of the ISO New England grid.
tldr: This paper proposes integrating fixed-point theorem-based network constraints into large-scale power grid capacity expansion optimization to account for AC optimal power flow while maintaining tractability.
motivation: Traditional capacity expansion models use simplified constraints that neglect AC power flow details, potentially affecting investment decisions.
method: The authors extend the GenX model by embedding ACOPF considerations via fixed-point theorem-based constraints, preserving dimensionality and runtime.
result: Comparison with transport-based and full ACOPF models on the ISO New England grid shows modest runtime increases and improved network physical accuracy.
conclusion: The approach provides a computationally efficient way to incorporate realistic power flow constraints into large-scale capacity planning.

title: Symplectic Tiling Billiards On Complete Affine Tori
authors: Fabian Lander Charles Daly
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28894v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In 2023, Richard Schwartz introduced a new dynamical system which is a marriage of two types of familiar billiards, tiling billiards and symplectic billiards. In this paper we investigate this dynamical system played on tilings of the plane which arise from non-Euclidean geometries on the torus. We review the affine analogue of the flat conformal structures on the torus through the work of Oliver Baues and William Goldman, and define an open subset of this deformation space corresponding to markings of complete affine tilings of the plane. We make this definition precise, and provide algebraic conditions on the symmetries of the tiling to define it. We then analyze the dynamics of symplectic tiling billiards played on these types of tilings and investigate the long-term dynamics of the system to prove a stability result concerning divergent trajectories. The divergence is defined in terms of geometric invariants arising from the tiling symmetry group. We argue that in some sense this divergence is a consequence of the tiles of a non-Euclidean tiling becoming 'thin' as one moves far away in the tiling. To do so we introduce a notion of thinness that is well adapted to the non-Euclidean affine tilings.
tldr: This paper studies the dynamics of symplectic tiling billiards on complete affine tori, proving a stability result about divergent trajectories.
motivation: The authors aim to understand a new dynamical system that combines tiling and symplectic billiards, specifically on non-Euclidean tilings of the torus.
method: They review affine conformal structures, define an open subset of the deformation space, and analyze the long-term dynamics of symplectic tiling billiards.
result: They prove a stability result concerning divergent trajectories, relating divergence to the thinness of tiles in non-Euclidean tilings.
conclusion: The divergence of trajectories is argued to be a consequence of the tiles becoming 'thin' far from the origin, providing geometric insight into the system.

title: A GPU-Accelerated Blocked Adaptive Randomized Range Finder Based On An Implicit Householder Qr Decomposition
authors: Andreas Herten Carolin Penke
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-rank methods can reduce the memory and computational requirements of deep neural network training in approaches such as GaLore. Randomized range finders offer an attractive alternative to singular value decompositions, particularly when the required rank is determined adaptively from a prescribed approximation tolerance. We introduce a blocked adaptive randomized range finder based on an implicit Householder QR decomposition and an optimized hybrid CPU--GPU implementation. The proposed method avoids explicit reorthogonalization. Numerical experiments show that it preserves orthogonality and approximation accuracy in regimes where block Gram--Schmidt without reorthogonalization becomes unstable. The blocked formulation exposes matrix--matrix operations and enables overlap of CPU panel factorization with GPU updates. On an NVIDIA GH200, the overlapped implementation reduces the runtime for the largest tested matrix from 9.91 seconds on the CPU to 0.407 seconds. The method provides a stable and efficient building block for low-rank approximation on heterogeneous systems with applications in computational science and engineering.
tldr: A GPU-accelerated blocked adaptive randomized range finder using implicit Householder QR, avoiding reorthogonalization, with significant speedups on hybrid CPU-GPU systems.
motivation: Low-rank methods can reduce memory and computational requirements in deep learning training (like GaLore); randomized range finders are attractive for adaptive rank determination, but need stable and efficient implementations.
method: Introduces a blocked adaptive randomized range finder based on implicit Householder QR decomposition, with an optimized hybrid CPU-GPU implementation, avoiding explicit reorthogonalization, and overlapping CPU panel factorization with GPU updates.
result: Preserves orthogonality and accuracy where block Gram-Schmidt fails; on NVIDIA GH200, reduces runtime from 9.91s (CPU) to 0.407s for largest matrix.
conclusion: Provides a stable and efficient building block for low-rank approximation on heterogeneous systems, applicable in computational science and engineering.

title: Minimizing The Arithmetic And Communication Complexity Of Jacobi's Method For Eigenvalues And Singular Values: Part Two -- Parallel Algorithms
authors: James Demmel, Hengrui Luo, Ryan Schneider, Yifu Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents several parallel versions of Jacobi's method for the symmetric eigenvalue problem and the SVD. A continuation of [Demmel, Luo, Schneider, & Wang 2025], we develop parallel Jacobi algorithms whose arithmetic cost is optimal and whose bandwidth or latency can match the corresponding lower bounds of parallel matrix multiplication. Our focus is a standard distributed-memory setting with variable processor layouts, including both 2D and 2.5D processor grids. In the 2D case, we demonstrate that a standard implementation of parallel Jacobi achieves a perfect speedup in arithmetic cost -- i.e., complexity [MATH] when done with [MATH] processors -- while hitting the 2D matrix-multiplication lower bound for bandwidth and (nearly) the lower bound for latency. By employing a 2.5D processor grid and leveraging 2.5D matrix multiplication, equivalently by increasing the memory per processor, we demonstrate that parallel Jacobi can achieve even lower bandwidth/latency, though we also prove that these costs cannot simultaneously match the best-known bounds for parallel matrix multiplication in any Jacobi algorithm. Finally, we extend our results to one-sided Jacobi SVD.
tldr: This paper proposes parallel Jacobi algorithms for eigenvalue and SVD problems that minimize arithmetic and communication costs in distributed-memory settings.
motivation: To develop numerically efficient parallel algorithms that simultaneously achieve optimal arithmetic cost and low communication overhead, matching lower bounds from matrix multiplication.
method: The authors analyze parallel Jacobi implementations on 2D and 2.5D processor grids, deriving complexity bounds and trade-offs between bandwidth, latency, and memory usage.
result: They show that standard parallel Jacobi achieves perfect arithmetic speedup and closely approaches communication lower bounds, but no Jacobi algorithm can match all optimal communication bounds simultaneously.
conclusion: The work extends to one-sided Jacobi SVD and provides a thorough complexity analysis, offering practical guidance for implementing communication-optimal parallel eigensolvers.

title: Mordukhovich Derivatives And Covering Constant For Set-Valued Metric Projection In General Banach Spaces
authors: Jinlu Li
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28961v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we find the explicit representation of the set-valued metric projection operator from l1 to the unit closed ball in l1. By using this representation, we investigate the properties of the Mordukhovich derivatives of the set-valued metric projection operator, which is applied to calculate its covering constant. As a special case, we consider the 2-d Banach space. We find the explicit solutions of the set-valued metric projection operator from the considered 2-d Banach space to its unit closed ball. By these solutions, we will calculate its Mordukhovich derivatives in details.
tldr: This paper studies the explicit form of set-valued metric projections in Banach spaces and computes their Mordukhovich derivatives and covering constants.
motivation: To characterize the differentiability and covering properties of metric projection operators in Banach spaces, specifically in l1 spaces.
method: By finding explicit representations of the projection operator and using them to compute Mordukhovich derivatives and covering constants.
result: Provides explicit formulas for the projection in l1 and 2-d Banach spaces, and calculates the corresponding derivatives.
conclusion: Contributes to nonsmooth analysis and approximation theory, but is unrelated to quantum information.

title: Calculus Of The Facial Distance
authors: Elias Wirth Javier Pena
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28971v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a few calculus rules to compute or lower bound the facial distance of a polytope. We illustrate our calculus rules on various popular polytopes. In particular, we provide a provide a lower bound on the facial distance of the Birkhoff polytope.
tldr: This paper develops calculus rules for computing or lower bounding the facial distance of polytopes, applying them to popular polytopes including the Birkhoff polytope.
motivation: The paper aims to provide tools for analyzing the geometry of polytopes, specifically the facial distance, which is important in combinatorial optimization.
method: The authors develop calculus rules to compute or bound the facial distance, and illustrate these rules on various polytopes.
result: They provide a lower bound on the facial distance of the Birkhoff polytope.
conclusion: The work contributes to the understanding of polytope geometry and offers computational methods for facial distance.

title: B$^3$-pwl: GPU-Batched Branch-and-Bound For Piecewise-Linear Optimization With Sos2 Constraints
authors: Yilin Guan, Shuqing Luo, Pingzhi Li, Tianlong Chen, Kaidi Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Piecewise-linear (PWL) optimization problems arise in many mixed-integer programming (MIP) optimization applications, including portfolio optimization, workforce scheduling, and resource allocation. But solving them to global optimality remains computationally expensive because branch-and-bound repeatedly solves LP relaxation subproblems. Existing solvers are largely CPU-centric, leaving the scalability of modern GPUs underutilized. Few prior GPU-accelerated branch-and-bound either targets neural network which is not suitable for general PWL optimization, or accelerates only auxiliary subroutines such as strong branching heuristics within CPU-centric MIP solvers. To bridge this gap, we propose B[MATH]-PWL, a GPU-centric batched branch-and-bound framework for piecewise-linear optimization with Special Ordered Set of type 2 (SOS2) constraints. Our method solves batches of LP relaxation subproblems concurrently on the GPU using a first-order primal-dual solver, enabled by a specialized batched block-tiled sparse matrix kernel. To complement bound computation, we further introduce a unified feasibility search module that combines an SOS2 repair primal heuristic with a batched feasibility pump to rapidly obtain feasible incumbents and improve pruning efficiency. On a benchmark of 43 PWL-MIP instances, B[MATH]-PWL achieves a 9.25x geometric-mean speedup over NVIDIA cuOpt while reaching high-quality feasible incumbents on every tested instance. On a public valve-point unit-commitment benchmark, it further outperforms NVIDIA cuOpt and the open-source CPU solvers SCIP and HiGHS, demonstrating the potential of first-order LP methods as the central engine of GPU-accelerated branch-and-bound.
tldr: This paper presents a GPU-accelerated batched branch-and-bound framework for solving piecewise-linear optimization problems with SOS2 constraints, achieving significant speedups over existing solvers.
motivation: Piecewise-linear optimization is computationally expensive due to repeated LP relaxations, and existing solvers are CPU-centric, underutilizing modern GPUs.
method: The method solves batches of LP relaxation subproblems concurrently on GPU using a first-order primal-dual solver with a specialized batched block-tiled sparse matrix kernel, and combines an SOS2 repair heuristic with a batched feasibility pump.
result: The framework achieves a 9.25x geometric-mean speedup over NVIDIA cuOpt on a benchmark of 43 instances and outperforms SCIP and HiGHS on a valve-point unit-commitment benchmark.
conclusion: GPU-centric first-order LP methods can serve as an effective central engine for branch-and-bound, demonstrating potential for general PWL optimization.

title: A New Primal-Dual Algorithm With Two Convex Combinations And Linesearch For General Convex-Concave Saddle-Point Problems
authors: Zexian Liu, Shuning Liu, Jialong Li
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28993v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Convex-concave saddle-point problems are ubiquitous across diverse domains, including machine learning, image processing, economics, and equilibrium problems. Primal-dual algorithms provide a highly effective and powerful framework for convex-concave saddle-point problems. Convex combination has become a crucial acceleration technique for primal-dual algorithms, and the integration of this technique has recently made these algorithms a highly active research topic. The choice of the convex combination parameter often has a significant impact on both the theoretical analysis and the numerical performance of the corresponding algorithms. However, the requirements on this parameter imposed by theory are sometimes inconsistent with those suggested by numerical experiments. For instance, theoretical analysis often requires the parameter to be small, while numerical experiments tend sometimes to favor larger values. To address this inconsistency and further advance primal-dual algorithms with convex combination, we develop a novel strategy based on two convex combinations, integrate it into a primal-dual framework, and propose a new primal-dual algorithm with linesearch, termed NPDAL-n, for general convex-concave saddle-point problems. The proposed two convex combinations in NPDAL-n ensure that the permissible range of the convex combination parameters is mainly determined by theoretical considerations, with little regard for numerical performance. Through rigorous Lyapunov energy descent analysis, we establish the global convergence and a sublinear ergodic convergence rate of [MATH] for NPDAL-n under standard assumptions. When the primal function is strongly convex, we develop an accelerated version of NPDAL-n that achieves an optimal [MATH] rate.
tldr: This paper presents a new primal-dual algorithm with two convex combinations and linesearch for convex-concave saddle-point problems, achieving sublinear convergence.
motivation: The authors address the inconsistency between theoretical requirements and numerical performance of convex combination parameters in primal-dual algorithms.
method: They propose NPDAL-n, integrating two convex combinations and linesearch, with Lyapunov energy descent analysis for convergence.
result: Global convergence and sublinear ergodic rate are established, with an optimal accelerated rate for strongly convex primal functions.
conclusion: The proposed algorithm improves parameter flexibility and convergence guarantees for saddle-point problems.

title: On The Existence Of Geometrically Attracting Measures For Iterated Function Systems With Varying Sets Of Transformations
authors: Dawid Czapla, Rafa{\l} Kapica, Maciej \'sl\k{e}czka
abstract: ArXiv:2608.29022v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we focus on the asymptotic behavior of random iterated functions systems, in which both the family of transformations and the distribution of selecting them vary at each step. We consider two types of dynamics: the time-inhomogeneous Markov chain arising from forward iterates and the non-Markovian process generated by backward iterates. For both settings, we provide certain criteria for the existence of a probability measure that is geometrically attracting in the bounded Lipschitz distance, independently of the initial distribution. Finally, we illustrate our results through applications to specific models involving affine transformations.
tldr: The paper investigates asymptotic behavior of random iterated function systems with time-varying transformations and selection distributions, proving criteria for existence of geometrically attracting measures.
motivation: To understand convergence properties of random iterated function systems when the system parameters change at each step, extending classical results to non-stationary settings.
method: Analyzes forward iterates as time-inhomogeneous Markov chains and backward iterates as non-Markovian processes, deriving conditions for geometric convergence in bounded Lipschitz distance.
result: Provides criteria for the existence of a probability measure that is geometrically attracting independently of the initial distribution, and applies them to affine transformation models.
conclusion: The results generalize existence of attracting measures to time-varying iterated function systems, confirmed through examples with affine maps.

title: DeepHSIC: Deep Learning-based Signal Detector For Hybrid Downlink Im-noma
authors: Dung Nguyen Tran, Toan D. Gian, Tien-Hoa Nguyen, Mai Xuan Trang, Tien-Cuong Nguyen, Thien van Luong
abstract: ArXiv:2608.29052v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: DeepHSIC is introduced as a neural receiver for hybrid downlink IM-NOMA transmission. The considered scheme combines power-domain NOMA with a composite OFDM/OFDM-IM waveform, so that user information is mapped jointly onto constellation symbols, subcarrier-index patterns, and different power levels. Although maximum-likelihood detection can achieve strong reliability for this model, its search space grows rapidly with the number of users and subcarriers. Conventional SIC reduces part of this burden, but its sequential cancellation may still accumulate errors and does not fully exploit the structure of IM-NOMA signals. To address this limitation, the proposed detector embeds dedicated deep neural network modules into the receiver and replaces the most computationally demanding SIC operations with learned inference blocks. The receiver is trained for Rayleigh fading channels and uses preprocessed channel-output features to recover user symbols. Simulation results show that DeepHSIC reaches BER performance close to model-based detectors under both perfect and imperfect CSI while requiring substantially lower detection time. These results indicate that learned SIC-style detection is a practical candidate for scalable hybrid downlink IM-NOMA receivers.
tldr: DeepHSIC is a deep learning-based receiver for hybrid downlink IM-NOMA that replaces SIC operations with neural networks, achieving performance close to model-based detectors with lower detection time.
motivation: Conventional SIC accumulates errors and does not fully exploit the structure of IM-NOMA signals, while maximum-likelihood detection suffers from high complexity. A learned detector is proposed to address these limitations.
method: The proposed detector embeds dedicated deep neural network modules to replace the most computationally demanding SIC operations, and is trained on Rayleigh fading channels using preprocessed channel-output features.
result: Simulation results show DeepHSIC reaches BER performance close to model-based detectors under both perfect and imperfect CSI while requiring substantially lower detection time.
conclusion: Learned SIC-style detection is a practical candidate for scalable hybrid downlink IM-NOMA receivers.

title: Neural Network-Based Delay-Doppler-Assisted Channel Estimation For Ofdm
authors: Mingcheng Nie, Hao Chang, Shuangyang Li, Haiyao Yu, Jiafu Hao, Yonghui Li
abstract: ArXiv:2608.29056v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) channel estimation relies on single-tap estimation and time-frequency (TF) interpolation, which becomes unreliable in high-mobility channels because Doppler-induced inter-carrier interference (ICI) invalidates the underlying element-wise TF model. This paper proposes a neural-network-based delay-Doppler (DD)-assisted channel estimation framework for OFDM over doubly selective channels. We first derive an ICI-aware TF domain input-output relation and formulate channel estimation as a DD recovery problem. Unlike conventional sparse recovery approaches, the proposed framework does not require the equivalent DD domain channel vector to be strictly sparse, thereby accommodating the leakage induced by fractional delay and Doppler shifts. Since the data symbols are unknown during channel estimation, the sensing matrix is constructed using only the known pilot symbols. As a result, data-induced interference is not explicitly modeled, leading to a structured mismatch in the pilot observations. To tackle this challenge, the adopted network iteratively exchanges observation- and channel-domain features through the sensing matrix to learn the mapping from these contaminated observations to the equivalent DD domain channel, which is subsequently used to reconstruct the TF-domain channel. Simulation results show that the proposed method achieves lower normalized mean-square error and bit-error rate than conventional OFDM estimators.
tldr: This paper proposes a neural network-based channel estimation framework for OFDM in high-mobility scenarios, leveraging the delay-Doppler domain to mitigate Doppler-induced inter-carrier interference.
motivation: Conventional OFDM channel estimation relying on single-tap estimation and time-frequency interpolation becomes unreliable in high-mobility channels due to Doppler-induced ICI, necessitating a more robust approach.
method: The method derives an ICI-aware time-frequency input-output relation, formulates channel estimation as a delay-Doppler recovery problem, and uses a neural network to iteratively learn the mapping from pilot observations to the equivalent delay-Doppler channel.
result: Simulation results show that the proposed method achieves lower normalized mean-square error and bit-error rate compared to conventional OFDM estimators.
conclusion: The neural-network-based delay-Doppler-assisted channel estimation effectively handles fractional delay and Doppler shifts without requiring strict sparsity, offering improved performance in doubly selective channels.

title: A Learnable Multigrid Framework Via Graph Convolutions
authors: Li Luo Xiuping Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.29082v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a novel framework that integrates learnable graph convolutions with the geometric multigrid method for solving partial differential equations (PDEs). The discretization of PDEs is first represented as a graph structure, enabling the application of graph convolutions to enhance the multigrid performance. By incorporating graph convolutions into the multigrid components such as smoothing and inter-grid transfer operators, we develop a learnable multigrid that can adaptively optimize its performance based on the underlying problem characteristics. In this framework, the graph convolutions are embedded directly within the multigrid cycle, effectively transforming the entire multigrid solver into a specialized neural network architecture, rather than combining a classical solver with surrogate models. The learnable multigrid framework is lightweight in terms of parameter count and requires minimal training effort to achieve good performance. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in solving some challenging problems, showing improved convergence rates compared to traditional multigrid methods. The generalizability of the learned parameters across different problem settings, including varying source terms, coefficients, geometries, and mesh sizes, is also investigated with proper weight-sharing and transfer-learning strategies.
tldr: This paper proposes a learnable multigrid framework that integrates graph convolutions into the multigrid cycle for solving partial differential equations, achieving improved convergence rates with generalizability across problem settings.
motivation: Traditional multigrid methods require problem-specific tuning; this work aims to adaptively optimize multigrid components using graph convolutions.
method: The PDE discretization is represented as a graph, and graph convolutions are embedded into smoothing and inter-grid transfer operators within the multigrid cycle, effectively turning the solver into a neural network architecture.
result: Numerical experiments show improved convergence rates compared to traditional multigrid, and the learned parameters generalize across source terms, coefficients, geometries, and mesh sizes using weight-sharing and transfer learning.
conclusion: The proposed framework is lightweight and requires minimal training effort, demonstrating a promising direction for learnable solvers.

title: Convergence Analysis Of Parametric Probabilistic Manifold Decomposition
authors: Dunhui Xiao Jiaming Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2608.29105v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a convergence analysis for a newly developed nonlinear model reduction method: parametric probabilistic manifold decomposition (PPMD)~. In addition, existing analyzes of nonlinear reduced order models typically treat subspace reduction, manifold representation, regression, and nonlinear reconstruction as separate components and often remain at the level of discrete state vectors. To the best of our knowledge, no theory tracks the complete error propagation in a data-dependent model whose basis, residual geometry, spectral coordinates, parameter maps, and lifting operator are all learned from the same numerical solution data. We develop a coupled perturbation analysis for the entire PPMD procedure. A trajectory geometry induced by the spatial discretization and temporal quadrature connects discrete trajectory vectors isometrically with the corresponding PDE norm. Population spectral objects are introduced to align the empirical residual coordinates and derive a uniform coordinate error estimate, whose propagation through the Hilbert-valued kernel lifting estimator is then quantified. Combining these results with the full order discretization error, weighted low-rank approximation, parameter regression, and residual representation defect yields deterministic and high-probability trajectory error bounds and consistency in probability in the continuous PDE trajectory space. The theory identifies how the principal errors interact and which components limit the accuracy of the nonlinear reduced order model.
tldr: This paper provides a convergence analysis for a nonlinear model reduction method called parametric probabilistic manifold decomposition (PPMD), focusing on error propagation in data-dependent reduced order models.
motivation: Existing analyses of nonlinear reduced order models treat components separately and lack a complete error propagation theory when all components are learned from the same data. The authors aim to provide a unified framework to understand error interactions and identify limiting factors.
method: The authors develop a coupled perturbation analysis for the entire PPMD procedure, using trajectory geometry, population spectral objects, and Hilbert-valued kernel lifting estimators to derive uniform coordinate error estimates and quantify error propagation.
result: The analysis yields deterministic and high-probability trajectory error bounds and consistency in probability in the continuous PDE trajectory space, identifying how principal errors interact and which components limit accuracy.
conclusion: The paper establishes a comprehensive theoretical foundation for PPMD, enabling better understanding and improvement of nonlinear reduced order models for PDEs.

title: The Stochastic Team Orienteering Problem
authors: Alberto Guastalla, Jean-Fran\c{c}ois C\^ot\'e, Roberto Aringhieri
abstract: ArXiv:2608.29119v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper analyses the Stochastic Team Orienteering Problem (STOP), a stochastic variant of the Team Orienteering Problem (TOP). In the STOP, travel times are represented by random variables. The objective is to determine a set of routes that maximises the expected collected profit. We model the problem as a two-stage stochastic integer program and propose an exact solution method based on the Integer L-shaped method. We also consider a set of non-linear chance constraints to restrict the search to highly reliable routes. In the first-stage, a set of routes is selected, while in the second-stage the recourse evaluates the expected profit of the selected routes. We present a new set of optimality cuts and strengthen the formulation by considering valid inequalities and constraints liftings. Computational results provide a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm using the standard TOP benchmark dataset from the literature.
tldr: This paper studies the Stochastic Team Orienteering Problem, a routing problem with stochastic travel times, and proposes an exact solution method based on integer L-shaped cuts and chance constraints.
motivation: The problem is an extension of the deterministic Team Orienteering Problem, addressing uncertainty in travel times to maximize expected collected profit.
method: The authors model it as a two-stage stochastic integer program, propose Integer L-shaped optimality cuts, strengthen with valid inequalities and liftings, and incorporate non-linear chance constraints for reliability.
result: Computational experiments on standard benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, providing comprehensive comparisons.
conclusion: The work contributes an exact solution approach for the Stochastic Team Orienteering Problem, advancing the state of the art in stochastic routing optimization.

title: A Tensor Neural Network Method For High-Order Homogenization Of Locally Periodic Elliptic Problems
authors: Huaijia Zhang, Haochen Liu, Xia Ji, Hehu Xie
abstract: ArXiv:2608.29176v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a high-order tensor neural network (TNN) method for locally periodic elliptic multiscale problems of the form [MATH]. Because the coefficient depends on both the slow variable [MATH] and the fast periodic variable [MATH], the high-order cell problems and macroscopic corrector equations are more involved than in the classical case [MATH], and the correctors depend parametrically on [MATH]. We derive a computable high-order two-scale expansion and prove an [MATH] convergence estimate for the partial expansion in boundary-layer-free settings, including periodic domains and ideal boundary-matching configurations. The proof uses the recursive compatibility structure of the corrector hierarchy and a zero-mean oscillation estimate in [MATH]. We then construct a TNN framework for the high-dimensional corrector problems. Its tensor-product structure permits deterministic one-dimensional quadrature for the cell problems, homogenized coefficients, macroscopic source terms, and loss functions, avoiding Monte Carlo integration error. The numerical realization assumes that the coefficient entries and assembled data admit finite or controlled tensor-product representations; this computational assumption is separate from the general matrix-valued coefficient class used in the analysis. Experiments with scalar locally periodic coefficients show accurate high-order correctors. The [MATH] semi-norm errors are consistent with the proved estimate, while point-normalized [MATH] errors display the nominal high-order behavior predicted by the formal expansion.
tldr: This paper develops a tensor neural network method for high-order homogenization of locally periodic elliptic problems, a numerical analysis topic unrelated to quantum information.
motivation: The authors aim to efficiently solve high-order cell problems and macroscopic corrector equations for locally periodic elliptic multiscale problems, which are computationally challenging.
method: They derive a computable high-order two-scale expansion and prove convergence, then construct a tensor neural network (TNN) framework exploiting tensor-product structure for deterministic quadrature.
result: Numerical experiments with scalar locally periodic coefficients show accurate high-order correctors, with errors consistent with the proved estimate.
conclusion: The TNN method offers an efficient approach for high-order homogenization problems, but is outside the scope of quantum information research.

title: Regularized Extragradient Method For Structured Bilevel Optimization In Continuous And Discrete Time
authors: Radu Ioan Bot, Enis Chenchene, David Alexander Hulett
abstract: ArXiv:2608.29181v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a real Hilbert space, we study a bilevel optimization problem that consists in minimizing an outer convex function over the zero set of a maximally monotone operator. In the smooth setting, where the outer objective is convex and Fr\'echet differentiable and the inner operator is single-valued, continuous and monotone, we associate with the problem a first-order dynamical system that can be viewed as a monotone flow applied to a dynamically regularized operator. Under suitable geometric conditions on the inner problem --- either a weak Attouch-Czarnecki-type integrability condition or the stronger assumption of sharpness --- we establish last-iterate convergence rates for both the outer and inner residuals, together with weak convergence of the trajectories to optimal solutions of the bilevel problem. In the smooth+nonsmooth setting, we enrich the outer objective with a proper, convex, and lower semicontinuous function, while the inner operator is augmented by the subdifferential of a function with the same properties.
